draft.title: Measuring unemployment in Australia
card: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) runs the Labour Force Survey each month. It asks a sample of households about work, then uses the answers to estimate unemployment for the whole country.
a person aged 15 or over who did at least one hour of paid work in the survey week.
a person with no paid work in the survey week who looked for work and could start work. Someone who has not looked for work is not counted as unemployed.
Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100. The labour force is everyone who is employed or unemployed.
draft.remember: To be unemployed, a person must have no work, be looking for work and be able to start.

a.q: Sam has no paid work, has sent job applications this month and could start next week. How does the ABS Labour Force Survey count Sam?
opts: Unemployed
Employed
Not in the labour force
Underemployed
a.why: Sam had no paid work, looked for work and could start, so Sam meets every test for unemployed. Sam is not outside the labour force, because that group is made of people who are not looking for work.
a.clue: Check Sam against all three tests for unemployed.

b.q: In the survey week, Priya had no paid job and did not look for work, though she wanted one. Tom did two hours of paid work and also looked for more. How does the survey count them?
opts: Priya is not unemployed and Tom is employed
Priya is unemployed and Tom is employed
Priya is not unemployed and Tom is unemployed
Priya is unemployed and Tom is unemployed
b.why: Priya did not look for work, so she fails one test and is not counted as unemployed, even though she wants a job. Tom did paid work in the survey week, so he is employed, even though he is looking for more.
b.clue: Wanting a job is not the same as looking for one.

b.best: Priya is not unemployed and Tom is employed

problems.detail: The question says Sam 'could start next week' and applied 'this month'. The ABS tests are about being available in the survey week and looking in the past four weeks. Since the question gives no survey week, 'next week' is loosely timed against the card's test. 'Could start now' would be cleaner.

Why (a) says people not in the labour force are 'people who are not looking for work'. That group also includes people who are looking but cannot start. The explanation should say they fail the looking test or the availability test.

proposal.title: Measuring unemployment in Australia
card: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) runs the Labour Force Survey each month. It asks a sample of households about work, then uses the answers to estimate unemployment for the whole country.
a person aged 15 or over who did at least one hour of paid work in the survey week.

a person aged 15 or over with no paid work in the survey week, who looked for work in the past four weeks and could start in the survey week. Someone who has not looked for work is not counted as unemployed.
Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100. The labour force is everyone who is employed or unemployed. Anyone 15 or over who is neither is not in the labour force.
proposal.remember: To be unemployed, a person must have no work, be looking for work and be able to start.

a.q: In the survey week, Sam had no paid work. Sam has applied for jobs over the past month and could start now. How does the ABS Labour Force Survey count Sam?
opts: Unemployed, and part of the labour force
Unemployed, but not part of the labour force
Not in the labour force, because Sam has no job
Employed, because Sam is actively seeking work
a.why: Sam had no paid work, looked for work in the past four weeks and could start now, so Sam meets all three tests for unemployed. Everyone who is unemployed is part of the labour force. People outside it are those who fail the looking test or the availability test, not those who simply have no job.
a.clue: Check Sam against all three tests, then recall who makes up the labour force.

b.clue: Wanting a job is not the same as looking for one.
